extracted.intended_audience: students, researchers, and general readers interested in digital culture, communication, and Internet memes
extracted.subtask_description: Framework and criteria for defining, analyzing, and explaining Internet memes: their properties, repackaging mechanisms, genres, success factors (memetic vs viral), political functions, and globalization dynamics. Intended as a primer for scholarly and applied study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author's definition of Internet memes
rubrics_metrics.description: An Internet meme is (a) a group of digital items sharing common characteristics of content, form, and/or stance; (b) that were created with awareness of each other; and (c) were circulated, imitated, and/or transformed via the Internet by many users.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this tripartite definition to identify memes (look for a corpus of related items rather than a single isolated item). Examples: Gangnam Style variants, ‘Hitler’s Downfall’ parodies. Emphasize shared content/form/stance, mutual awareness among variants, and broad online circulation/derivative creation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dawkins's memetic success properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful memes incorporate three basic properties—longevity, fecundity, and copy fidelity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longevity: ability to persist over time; Fecundity: rate/number of copies produced; Copy fidelity: accuracy of replication. In digital contexts all three are enhanced (lossless transfer, rapid diffusion, indefinite archival). Use these as high-level success metrics when comparing memetic items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Micro–macro propagation (scaling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Memes spread gradually from individuals to society, scaling from micro acts of imitation to macro shared social phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether individual acts (uploads, remixes) aggregate into a visible corpus that shapes group mindsets or behavior. A meme’s social impact is a key criterion, not only raw views.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproduction via copying and imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Memes reproduce through copying, imitation, repackaging; digital affordances often allow exact forwarding or inspired re-creation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how a piece invites replication (can it be forwarded unchanged, mimicked, remixed?). Two main repackaging mechanisms: mimicry (redoing/re-creation) and remix (technology-based manipulation like Photoshop or soundtrack changes). Examples: YouTube emulations, Photoshopped image variants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diffusion through competition and selection (fitness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Memes vary in fitness—adaptability to their sociocultural environment—and spread through competition and selective adoption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine factors that make variants more 'fit' (relevance, interpretive openness, visibility). In digital contexts metadata (views, likes) becomes part of selection processes; people consider popularity signals before adopting/remixing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intertextuality
rubrics_metrics.description: Memes often relate to each other in complex, creative, and surprising ways (blending, referencing, combining distinct memes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for cross-meme references (e.g., ‘Gangnam Style’ + ‘Binders Full of Women’ → hybrid variants). Intertextual links are evidence of memetic networks and meaning-making across items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visibility and traceability of memetic variability
rubrics_metrics.description: In digital environments the corpus of meme variants and their timelines are visible and searchable—visibility of variants is itself a memetic attribute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how easily a researcher or user can observe the family of variants (searchability, tag use, hosted archives). The visible corpus is often integral to the meme’s cultural function and study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performative self / personal branding in memetic artifacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Many Internet memes—especially videos and photos—foreground the uploader/performer, making the self both medium and message (self-commodification).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing or producing memetic content, note whether personal visibility (faces, bodies, personas) is central; this often aligns with network individualism and identity signaling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypermemetic logic: attention and sharing as value
rubrics_metrics.description: Contemporary meme culture is embedded in an attention economy and a sharing logic—spreading and derivative creation are culturally valued activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use attention (views, shares, derivatives) and prestige/positioning as evaluative dimensions. Consider seeding strategies, positioning, and prestige-seeking behaviors that drive memetic engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mimicry versus remix (repackaging mechanisms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two central repackaging strategies: mimicry (re-creating an original text/action) and remix (technologically altering an original, e.g., Photoshop, soundtrack changes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify derivatives by mechanism; mimicry often emphasizes performance/replication, remix emphasizes creative transformation. Both indicate memetic uptake but imply different participatory skill sets and aesthetics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content characteristics of memetic videos
rubrics_metrics.description: Common features of memetic videos include focus on ordinary people, flawed masculinity themes, humor (verbal/visual), repetitiveness, simplicity, whimsy, and audiovisual incongruity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing or producing memetic videos, assess simplicity of concept, repetitiveness (catchy hooks), humor type (superiority, incongruity), ordinary-person appeal, and whether audiovisual mismatches create comedic effect (e.g., ‘Charlie Bit My Finger’, ‘Gangnam Style’ derivatives).

rubrics_metrics.name: Content characteristics of memetic photos / image macros
rubrics_metrics.description: Memetic photos often rely on frozen motion, image juxtaposition, visual puzzles/incompleteness, and easily reproducible image templates (e.g., reaction Photoshops, image macros, LOLcats).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate visual incongruity, gap/incompleteness (inviting interpretation), and ease of re-editing (templated formats). Such features increase memetic potential and derivative creation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and repeatability
rubrics_metrics.description: Simplicity (a clear, easy-to-reproduce form) and repetitiveness (catchy, repeatable elements) boost memetic replication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a piece is simple enough for broad imitation and contains repetitive hooks that facilitate easy copying or parody (melodies, gestures, captions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Incompleteness / puzzles as invitations to participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Gaps, puzzles, or open meanings (incompleteness) elicit memetic responses as users seek to 'complete' or reinterpret the item.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify whether the content leaves interpretive space (mystery, ambiguous meaning) that encourages derivatives and user engagement (e.g., Kilroy’s mysterious slogan).

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional arousal and positivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Emotional arousal (surprise, sadness, joy) influences virality; positivity and humor are often associated with sharing and memetic uptake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating persuasive or viral potential, measure emotional appeal—positive/empathic content often spreads via personalized sharing, but high-arousal negative content can also go viral depending on context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Packaging and positioning
rubrics_metrics.description: How content is packaged (title, thumbnails, captions) and positioned (seeding strategies, prestige cues) matters for adoption and spread.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess metadata, framing, and seeding (who shares first, where it is posted). Effective packaging increases visibility and perceived prestige, which in turn influences selection and imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seeding strategies and hubs
rubrics_metrics.description: The initial placement of content (seeding) and distribution through meme hubs (YouTube, Reddit, Tumblr, 4chan, KnowYourMeme) strongly affect diffusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider platform affordances, community norms of hubs, and early adopters when evaluating memetic potential. Hubs have distinct cultures that shape what variants are produced and amplified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prestige and social positioning
rubrics_metrics.description: Prestige signals—who shares/endorses content—affect adoption; prestige can come from celebrity, influential communities, or platform prominence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate endorsements, celebrity involvement, and institutional attention as amplifiers of memetic spread; producers may target prestige nodes to seed a meme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre classification (meme genres)
rubrics_metrics.description: Memes fall into recognizable genres (flash mobs, lipdubs, LOLcats/image macros, misheard lyrics, reaction Photoshops, recut trailers, stock character macros, rage comics, photo fads, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify items by genre to compare forms and conventions; genres imply different production techniques, participant literacies, and community rules. Use genre conventions when creating derivatives (templates, tropes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Political meme functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Political memes can function as action (mobilization), discourse (framing public conversation), persuasion (influence), and participation (citizen engagement); they can also enable critical use and democratic subversion or be subject to censorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate political memes by intended function (call to action vs commentary), persuasive devices, ability to build collective identity, risks (backlash, censorship), and examples such as ‘Pepper-Spraying Cop,’ Occupy-related memes, or culture-jamming campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memes versus virals: distinguishing features
rubrics_metrics.description: While often used interchangeably, 'memes' and 'virals' differ: memetic items are defined as groups of related variants with intertextuality and imitation, whereas virals are often single items whose spread relies on packaging, emotional arousal, and participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this distinction when evaluating success: memetic success emphasizes derivative streams and genre formation; viral success emphasizes immediate reach, packaging, emotional hooks, and shareability. Compare content characteristics lists for both types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meme literacy and subcultural knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding a meme often requires subcultural literacy—knowledge of norms, references, and community-specific signs; reproduction creates bonds among 'in the know' participants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess required literacy level for participation; memes that rely on niche references will circulate within communities but may be less globally transmissible unless localized or recontextualized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Globalization and glocalization of memes
rubrics_metrics.description: Global memes often undergo localization (glocalization): translation, local references, and adaptation affect directionality and language dynamics in meme diffusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing global spread, examine how memes are adapted across languages/cultures, whether they reflect Americanization/Westernization, and how local reworkings alter meaning and uptake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes / functions of communication in memes
rubrics_metrics.description: Memetic items perform multiple communicative functions (poetic, phatic, emotive, conative, referential, metalingual) that influence how they are produced and interpreted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the dominant communication function (e.g., phatic sharing vs persuasive messaging) to understand user motivations and likely diffusion paths. Jakobson's functions can be used as analytic lenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Countermemes and culture-jamming as evaluative responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Memes can be countered by countermemes, culture-jamming, or critical remixes; such responses are part of memetic politics and evaluative dynamics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether content spawns countermemes (opposition variants) and how that affects public discourse, persuasion, and censorship. Countermemes may reveal contested meanings and audience segmentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical and political constraints (censorship, repression)
rubrics_metrics.description: Memetic circulation is shaped by political contexts: censorship, repression, and platform moderation alter diffusion and creative strategies (e.g., coded symbols, euphemisms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider legal/political risks and local platform rules when producing or analyzing political memes; creative evasions (coded language, homophones) may indicate constrained publics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research and analytic traceability
rubrics_metrics.description: Digital traces (metadata, view counts, timestamps, tags) enable empirical tracing of meme spread and variant evolution—useful for rigorous analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage platform metadata to chart propagation timelines, hubs, influential spreaders, and variant genealogies. Traceability is a methodological criterion for memetic research quality.
